extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners designing reviewer-assignment systems (conference chairs, journal editors, grant program managers, and computer scientists working on RAP)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, evaluating, and improving automated reviewer-assignment (RAP) systems for conferences, journals, and grant programs, including similarity computation, COI detection, and optimization of assignments. Covers data collection, model choices (text/network/ML), evaluation metrics, fairness and re-optimization strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish comprehensive and reliable reviewer and proposal databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing comprehensive and reliable reviewer and proposal databases is essential to ensure accurate proposal-reviewer matching. It is common to use static databases of manually collected and not updated information; dynamic databases (e.g., OpenReview, DBLP) contain structured or unstructured data from multiple sources but need improved accuracy and completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and continuously update reviewer profiles and proposal metadata from multiple sources; prefer rich dynamic data but invest effort to improve accuracy and completeness. Maintain structured fields (affiliation, publications, keywords, coauthorship) to support matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute similarity scores for every proposal–reviewer pair
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary goal of stage 2 is to calculate a similarity score for every possible proposal-reviewer pair based on the profile of candidate reviewers and proposals. Existing approaches fall into manual, text-based (NLP), and network-based categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose similarity methods appropriate to available data; compare manual, text-based, and network-based approaches; evaluate impact of similarity accuracy on downstream assignment quality; consider automation via NLP to scale scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply neural network-based / transformer pre-trained language models for similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Neural network-based language models (particularly transformer-based pre-trained models such as XLNet, RoBERTa, and T5) offer potent feature extraction capabilities that can aid in enhancing the similarity score accuracy between proposals and reviewers. Few RAP studies have yet reached consensus on their benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with next-generation embedding models vs semantic/word-based methods; assess gains in relevance and robustness. Note dependency on domain-specific training data; where possible, fine-tune or adapt pre-trained models to the domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require large domain-specific training datasets for ML similarity methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-trained language models can be directly used to assign reviewers based on large amounts of proposal/reviewer data, but the quality of results depends on availability of extensive domain-specific training data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers and review organizers should collaborate to create and share large domain-specific datasets to improve supervised/transfer learning performance; consider anonymization and privacy when sharing sensitive data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop hybrid similarity methods combining word and semantic information
rubrics_metrics.description: Some studies use word and semantic information together and report better results than using either alone. Future work should develop additional hybrid methods for calculating similarity scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate lexical (TF-IDF, keywords) and semantic (embeddings, topic models) features; evaluate trade-offs in speed, interpretability, and accuracy. Consider combining text-based, network-based, and manual signals for robustness and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use network-based models to exploit implicit relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Network-based models (coauthorship, citation, social/affiliation networks) analyze implicit relationships and strengthen reviewer recommendation while helping to avoid potential COIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate co-authorship and citation networks into similarity/constraint computations; evaluate how network proximity correlates with expertise and COI risk. Combine network and text signals to improve matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatically detect conflicts of interest (COIs) using multiple relationship types
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior studies primarily detect COIs via weighted connections such as co-author and citation networks. Other social/academic relationships (advisee–advisor, competitors, project collaborators) may also create COIs that are not captured by publication links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand COI detection beyond coauthorship/citation to include advisor–advisee, colleague, project collaboration, and competitive relationships. Use supervised learning where possible, but note the lack of high-quality ground-truth COI datasets; prioritize building such datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build interactive COI extraction and declaration systems (e.g., PISTIS)
rubrics_metrics.description: For accurate COI detection, it is required to build interactive systems that can automatically extract latent COIs from open sources and contain declaration modules for subjective COI categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy systems that combine automated extraction (from public sources) with human/declarative inputs to capture subjective COIs. Provide interfaces for reviewers/applicants to declare nuanced relationships and for organizers to inspect extracted signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt flexible COI avoidance strategies rather than blanket bans
rubrics_metrics.description: Although it is generally believed a reviewer with existing COIs should not be assigned to the proposal, a universal approach can leave insufficient qualified reviewers in scarce areas. Flexible COI avoidance strategies can consider types and degrees of COIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop policies that differentiate COI types and degrees (e.g., recent close collaboration vs distant shared advisor). Allow controlled exceptions when expertise is scarce, guided by measured COI strength and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure degree/strength of relationships to quantify COI risk
rubrics_metrics.description: How to measure the strength of relationships that lead to COIs has been seldom concerned; distance in relationship networks can be utilized to estimate the degree of COIs (closer nodes imply stronger COI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and validate metrics (graph distance, weighted path strength, recency/volume of collaboration) to quantify COI risk; calibrate thresholds for assignment decisions and investigate supervised COI scoring models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire and consolidate diverse social network data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential to acquire and consolidate social networks from a variety of sources (advisee–advisor, affiliation/colleague networks, project collaborators) so that different relationship types are reflected and the massive dataset can be examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate multiple relationship data sources, resolve entity disambiguation, and harmonize representations. Address privacy and sensitivity; use consolidated networks to improve both similarity and COI detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid maximizing overall similarity as sole objective — ensure per-proposal expertise minima
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximizing overall similarity is common but can lead to injustice for some proposals (e.g., being assigned to reviewers lacking topical expertise). Ensuring each proposal is assigned to a group of reviewers with minimum acceptable expertise is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate constraints for minimum proximity/expertise per proposal or optimize worst-case proximities; consider constrained optimization formulations (minimax, lower-bound constraints). Balance global objective vs per-proposal fairness; be mindful of computational complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve computational efficiency of constrained/robust optimization approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Strict constraints or worst-case optimization approaches to ensure fairness are difficult to solve due to complexity. Future research should enhance computing efficiency of these approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop scalable algorithms (approximation, heuristics, re-optimization routines) or decomposition methods to handle large-scale RAPs with fairness constraints; evaluate trade-offs between optimality and runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop re-optimization strategies for late-discovered COIs or unqualified reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: When unknown COIs are discovered or a reviewer is found severely unqualified, new reviewers must be identified and a new decision-making procedure implemented. In time-constrained contexts, re-optimization approaches are preferable to repeating the entire procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incremental/fast re-optimization methods that update assignments with minimal disruption (local search, swap-based heuristics, constrained reruns). Include fallbacks for emergency reassignment and quantify impact on load/fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamically optimize assignments including reviewer feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving feedback from reviewers can improve reviewer satisfaction and result in more accurate reviewer–proposal matches. Future research should explore dynamically optimizing assignments using reviewers’ feedback on assignment results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate feedback loops (post-assignment satisfaction, self-reported expertise, bidding) into iterative assignment procedures; use online learning or adaptive matching to refine future similarity estimations and assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate techniques across all RAP stages instead of siloed solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most RAP studies focus on one or two stages; techniques for resolving different phases are rarely coordinated. Assignment outcomes depend heavily on similarity-calculation accuracy, so end-to-end methods that consider all three stages are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design integrated pipelines that jointly consider profile construction, similarity scoring, and optimization; measure how improvements in one stage affect others. Explore joint modeling approaches and multi-stage optimization frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage collaborative and historical feedback across iterations
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether similarity measurement and reviewer assignment can be addressed collaboratively, possibly including feedback from previous issues of the conference/journal or earlier iterations of grant programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical assignment/outcome data to inform current similarity models (learning-to-rank, calibration), and allow community input to refine criteria. Maintain versioned models and track longitudinal performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardize reviewer assignment criteria and procedures per area
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts should be made to establish standardized reviewer assignment criteria and procedures for each area to ensure accuracy and fairness of the assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop domain-specific standards (minimum expertise thresholds, acceptable COI definitions, required profile fields) and documented procedures for assignment. Promote adoption via community bodies (conferences, journals, funders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and publish well-designed benchmark datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: Most real datasets used to evaluate RAP methods are not publicly accessible due to sensitive information, preventing direct comparison. The absence of a standard benchmark impedes comparing approaches; therefore, a collection of well-designed benchmark datasets should be established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct anonymized, representative benchmark datasets with documented provenance and evaluation protocols; include synthetic and real-world variants; provide baseline tasks and metrics to enable reproducible comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standardized evaluation metrics for similarity and assignment quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies use a wide variety of performance metrics (precision, recall, accuracy, F-score, macro-F1, mean average precision, normalized discounted cumulative gain, DCG, RMSE, MAE, MAPE, coverage, authority, diversity, matching degree, load variance, expertise variance, computational time, objective function value, quality, perplexity, KL divergence, entropy, suitability score, confidence measures, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose evaluation metrics aligned with goals (relevance accuracy, fairness, load balance, runtime). Report multiple complementary metrics (relevance plus fairness and runtime). Adopt standard metrics (e.g., MAP, NDCG for ranking; precision/recall/F1; computational time and solution quality for optimization) to allow cross-study comparisons.
